transcript:
[00:00] Sam Park: alright everyone thanks for joining, we'll kick off the weekly poc sync on throughput optimization. we have maya with me from the se team.
[00:08] Alex Rivera: hey Sam, hey Maya, good to be back. quick morning for us.
[00:12] Maya Chen: hi all, quick agenda — review last week's runs, look at continuous batching changes, concurrency sweep plan, and next steps.
[00:20] Priya Singh: sounds good, i uploaded the new prompt sample to the shared folder this morning — it's a bit noisy but represents our mix.
[00:26] Sam Park: perfect, thanks priya. okay maya, can you summarize the perf numbers?
[00:30] Maya Chen: yeah so baseline run last monday on the hosted variant using 4xA100 instances, we saw tokens per second around 48k with default batching window 10ms. after we increased window to 30ms and set max_batch to 128 we jumped to ~61k tps. p50 latency was fine but p95 moved from 180ms to 260ms and p99 spiked to 620ms, primarily on short prompt requests.
[01:00] Tom Brooks: so we gained throughput at the cost of tail latency, which matches what we'd expect. for our UX the p99 on small requests is more problematic than aggregate tps improvement.
[01:10] Alex Rivera: yeah our payment auth flow has many short calls and a 500ms tail is a dealbreaker for some flows.
[01:18] Maya Chen: right, this is classic batching tradeoff. you can tune dynamic early flush — if you detect small request population you flush earlier or route them to a low-latency pool. we have two knobs: reduction of batching window and also concurrency per GPU.
[01:30] Sam Park: remind me again of our target throughput and allowed p99?
[01:34] Priya Singh: target is 300 TPS sustained for the auth surface, with median token latency under 20ms for small prompts and p99 under 250ms ideally.
[01:44] Maya Chen: ok so we need to reduce the tail. three approaches we discussed: 1) reduce batch window and use more concurrency so batches are naturally smaller, 2) use request sizing route to send small prompts to a low-latency lane (separate model variant or fewer batching), 3) server-side queue throttle that prioritizes short requests.
[02:00] Tom Brooks: concurrency — is that per GPU thread or per model replica? what's the limit before we see GPU saturation?
[02:06] Maya Chen: good question. concurrency is per replica, so if you set concurrency 32 on a single GPU-backed worker it will accept up to 32 inflight requests. beyond a point kernels contend for memory bandwidth and throughput can plateau or drop. our plan is to sweep 8, 16, 32 to see where tokens/sec and p99 cross. last month we saw 16 was sweet spot for this model architecture on that instance class.
[02:26] Alex Rivera: and continuous batching — can it early-flush by request count or latency?
[02:30] Maya Chen: yes, early flush rules: max wait time (ms), max batch size, and a fast-path for small requests using size heuristics. you can also configure to flush if low-latency requests are pending. it's not perfect with transcription hiccups, but it's stable.
[02:44] Priya Singh: another note, our prompt mix is heavier on short prompts in peak windows — about 72% under 60 tokens, 20% medium, 8% long. that skews p99.
[02:54] Maya Chen: that helps, thanks priya. so my action is to run the concurrency sweep with current prompt mix and log p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec and memory utilization.
[03:02] Sam Park: great. any updates on the dedicated pool cost query?
[03:05] Maya Chen: sam i ran a quick estimate — a 4-GPU dedicated pool with the A100-class hardware we used in staging will be about $Xk/month, depends on sustained concurrency and reserved commit. i'll send exact numbers and a comparison to hosted per-token costs.
[03:18] Alex Rivera: if we go dedicated we need VPC peering and egress rules; tom will share details of net egress and our firewall.
[03:24] Tom Brooks: yes i'll export the network diagrams and baseline. also we may have TLS interception on some of our egress which might affect keepalives.
[03:32] Sam Park: ok noted. on queueing, we discussed client-side queuing and server-side rate limits. for fairness and backpressure we recommend server-side soft queue with token budget enforcement plus client retries with jitter. this prevents head-of-line blocking.
[03:44] Priya Singh: do you have an example config? something we can drop into our test harness?
[03:48] Maya Chen: yes i'll put the sample config in the shared folder — it includes concurrency, batch window, early flush thresholds, and a two-lane routing rule for small vs large prompts.
[03:58] Alex Rivera: one more question — how do you measure cost per effective request with batching? we need to know unit economics when we compare hosted vs dedicated.
[04:06] Maya Chen: good point. we measure token costs then divide by effective answered requests per second. batching improves tokens/sec but also increases tokens per request slightly in some cases because of padding; we'll provide a breakdown: per-token compute cost, overhead due to padding, and net cost per successful response.
[04:22] Tom Brooks: in the previous run the padding overhead was fairly low because priya's prompt mix is short, but medium and long requests cause higher per-request token consumption.
[04:30] Sam Park: ok, let's talk schedule. maya will run sweep, priya to upload final prompt set, tom to send infra details. we'll reconvene next week to review numbers and discuss queueing deep dive.
[04:40] Priya Singh: quick clarifying question — for the concurrency sweep should we test both batch window 10ms and 30ms or just one?
[04:46] Maya Chen: do both. run 10ms and 30ms at each concurrency point so we can see interaction. i'll provide the run matrix.
[04:54] Alex Rivera: perfect. also can you include the config to simulate burst traffic? we want to validate tail behavior under sudden spikes.
[04:59] Maya Chen: yes, include a 5-second burst pattern and a 60-second sustained pattern.
[05:04] Sam Park: any blockers on our side?
[05:06] Tom Brooks: none immediate, just need to align on network details.
[05:09] Maya Chen: i'll start runs today and should have initial numbers by friday.
[05:12] Sam Park: excellent. last thing — i'll send the cost estimate and the dedicated pool comparison after the call.
[05:18] Alex Rivera: thanks everyone, appreciate the focused run plan.
[05:20] Sam Park: thanks team, we'll follow up with the action item notes and shared folder links. end.
